transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump says major tech companies have agreed to come together and "self-police"
their AI products.
The voluntary agreement comes after about 30 executives from the biggest U.S. tech companies
gathered at the White House, and PR's Emily Feng has more.
Asked whether this agreement was legally enforceable, Trump replied.
I think it's morally binding, yeah.
He argued that private tech companies can be trusted to regulate themselves.
The accord asks companies to monitor their AI products and set up internal controls to
make sure they do not hack into other systems.
Their companies are at stake.
If something goes wrong, their companies are at stake, they're not going to let that happen.
This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe, and
they're really going to be policing each other.
Those involved offered no details on how that would work.
Emily Feng and PR News, the White House.
The Department of Homeland Security has tapped $20 million to pay for campaign-style ads
promoting President Trump.
The ads have drawn widespread criticism from Republicans and Democrats who call them a
blatant misuse of taxpayer dollars and likely illegal.
Democrats say Trump's budget director moved the money from Homeland Security to the ad
campaign earlier this month.
The FBI says authorities in the Netherlands have arrested a suspected leader of the cyber
criminal group that recently claimed to have hacked the FBI, and PR's Ryan Lucas reports
Dutch national police took the individual into custody this morning.
The FBI says the suspect is an alleged leader of the criminal hacking group Shiny Hunters.
That's the same group that last week claimed to have hacked the FBI jobs portal and stolen
private personal data and work information on thousands of current and former FBI employees.
In a video posted on X, FBI cyber official Brett Leatherman had this message for members
of Shiny Hunters.
The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you.
You know how to find us, and we know how to find you.
I suggest you reach out first while the choice is still yours.
The Shiny Hunter hack of the FBI jobs portal is an embarrassing episode for the bureau and
carries potentially serious counterintelligence and safety consequences.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
It would be illegal to try to make a baby using gene-edited human embryos in the United
States, but at least two startups are hoping to change that, and PR's Rob Stein has more.
Origin Genomics in New York City and Preventive Bio in San Francisco are trying to produce
enough evidence to convince regulators that it would be safe to use modified embryos for
reproduction.
The companies say gene-editing embryos could help millions of babies from being born with
rare but devastating genetic disorders.
Critics, however, warn it may never be safe and worry that allowing gene-editing of human
embryos for any reason could open the door to someone trying to go further and create
designer babies.
Rob Stein, NPR News.
Stocks drifted lower on Wall Street today.
This is NPR News.
Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California is retiring its X2 roller coaster after 20
years amid lawsuits alleging brain injuries.
Six Flags recently settled a wrongful death suit from the family of a 22-year-old who
died after riding the coaster in 2022.
Three more lawsuits alleging brain injuries were filed last week.
The CDC has added a second measles death in 2026 to its national tally, and PR's Maria
Godoy reports it comes after Pennsylvania reported four measles-associated deaths.
The CDC website did not identify where the death occurred, so it's unclear if the new
death is one of the four reported in Pennsylvania.
No other state has reported a measles-associated death this year.
The deaths have become wrapped up in a political feud between Pennsylvania's Democratic Governor
Josh Shapiro and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.
When Shapiro announced the first two deaths, Kennedy initially questioned whether they
were due to measles, and in a highly unusual move, the CDC initially excluded them from
its weekly measles tally.
The CDC says it's working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to
develop a standardized definition for deaths due to measles, Maria Godoy, NPR News.
Chicago native Pope Leo XIV sent a letter of encouragement to the Chicago White Sox
as they begin their postseason series against the Houston Astros today.
The letter acknowledged a game on August 11th where the team gave out "Pope hats" to
a sold-out crowd.
Leo is a Sox fan, but the Chicago Cubs have also made it to the playoffs.
It's only the fourth time in history both teams are in the postseason.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: President Trump announces major tech companies have agreed to self-police their AI products
Department of Homeland Security allocated $20 million for campaign-style ads promoting President Trump
FBI says Dutch authorities arrested suspected leader of Shiny Hunters cyber criminal group
Two biotech startups seek to legalize gene-edited human embryos for reproduction in U.S.
Stocks drifted lower on Wall Street today
Six Flags Magic Mountain retiring X2 roller coaster after 20 years amid injury lawsuits
CDC adds second measles death in 2026 to national tally, Pennsylvania reports four
Pope Leo XIV sends letter of encouragement to Chicago White Sox for postseason series
